query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A moderate increase in Cu content within the FeNiCrCoCu coating promotes the formation of an optimal, thin and coherent Cu-rich oxide layer during high-temperature sliding, which in turn serves as a protective barrier to reduce abrasive wear and limit severe plastic deformation relative to the baseline coating.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating with baseline Cu content deposited on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Systematically increase the Cu content (e.g., by approximately 10% relative to the baseline) in the HEA coating.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding wear conditions at approximately 600–800°C with comparable normal loads and sliding speeds.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an in situ developed, thin, Cu-rich oxide layer that forms coherently at the coating surface.
generation.mechanism: The increased Cu enhances selective oxidation under high-temperature frictional heat; this results in a protective oxide barrier that both retards excessive plastic deformation and provides beneficial work hardening. If the oxide remains thin and continuous, it reduces material loss, but if it grows too thick the wear performance might deteriorate.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified coating will exhibit a lower wear rate and reduced microscopic plastic deformation compared to the baseline under high-temperature sliding conditions due to the formation of a beneficial oxide layer.
generation.baseline: FeNiCrCoCu HEA coating with the original, unmodified Cu composition that does not promote the same optimal oxide layer formation.
generation.boundary: This outcome is expected under high-temperature sliding (600–800°C) and within a moderate range of Cu enhancement; results may differ outside this temperature range or with excessive Cu increases that could lead to overly thick or brittle oxide scales.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimum Cu increment and oxide thickness for peak performance is not fully established; additionally, the interplay between protective oxidation and potential brittle oxide spallation remains to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on identical substrates: one with the baseline Cu content and one with a moderate (approximately 10% increased) Cu content. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature sliding wear tests (600–800°C) under fixed load and sliding speed conditions. Subsequently, analyze the wear scars using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to evaluate oxide layer formation, quantify wear rates, and assess local plastic deformation via microhardness mapping.
measurements: Wear rate (volume loss per unit load and sliding distance)
Thickness, continuity, and composition of the in situ formed oxide layer
Extent of microscopic plastic deformation (e.g., via microhardness or surface profiling)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cu-enhanced coating does not show a statistically significant reduction in wear rate or plastic deformation compared to the baseline coating, or if a distinct Cu-rich oxide layer is not observed, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

With the continuous development of laser and mechanical technology, the application of laser cladding is more and more extensive [,]. In order to improve the wear resistance of common parts, a layer of material with better wear resistance is often prepared on the parts using laser cladding technology. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) with high hardness, outstanding wear resistance and excellent corrosion resistance [,,] are considered as promising materials in the fields of high-temperature-resistant alloys, wear-resistant alloys and corrosion-resistant alloys, etc. [,]. AbstractThe effect and mechanism of grain sizes on the tribological behavior of CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy (HEA) were studied by friction experiments and wear morphology analysis. Under normal low load and low sliding speed, the primary wear mechanism of the HEA samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the samples are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. The oxide layer formed under the action of friction heat of the coarse grain (CG) sample is easy to break due to the softening of the CG. With the increase of normal load and sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the HEA samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation. The oxide layer of CG sample has many cracks, and the worn surface also has plastic deformation, which leads to the increase of friction coefficient and specific wear rate and the decrease of wear resistance. Therefore, the fine grain size HEA sample has better wear resistance than the CG sample due to its high surface strength.Keywords: high entropy alloy, grain size, tribological behavior, wear mechanism

frame.system: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating on a conventional metal substrate in its baseline processing state
frame.goal: Develop a single, mechanistic and testable hypothesis that connects controlled compositional or microstructural changes to improved wear resistance and controlled microscopic deformation during high-temperature sliding.
frame.limitation: A lack of clear mechanistic understanding of how microstructure and in‐situ oxidation under high-temperature sliding conditions govern wear and deformation, particularly in balancing beneficial work hardening versus degradation from excessive oxide formation.
root_cause_cues: controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition
constraints: Must be a single testable mechanistic hypothesis
Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition
Predict directional changes in wear and deformation
State the regime (high-temperature sliding) in which predictions hold
Specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis
frame.regime: High-temperature sliding wear conditions (e.g., ~600–800°C) where both oxidation kinetics and thermal softening can affect the coating behavior
prior_attempts: Existing studies on HEA coatings have focused on compositional optimization and microstructural stability but have not directly correlated controlled modifications (e.g., subtle Cu content variation) with mechanistic outcomes in wear and deformation under high temperatures.

Prior research on similar alloys indicated that in-situ oxidation can be both beneficial (creating a protective layer) and detrimental (if the oxide is too thick), but a process–structure–property relationship was not established in a controlled, comparative change from a defined baseline.
frame.understanding: The hypothesis proposes that a controlled increase in Cu content (or another element that promotes selective oxidation) in the FeNiCrCoCu HEA creates an optimal, in-situ developed oxide layer under high-temperature sliding conditions. This oxide layer provides a dual function: it acts as a barrier to severe plastic deformation and wear while simultaneously facilitating beneficial work hardening in the near-surface region. The controlled change (i.e., a slight deliberate increase in Cu relative to baseline) is expected to lower overall wear rates and reduce microscopic deformation. However, if the oxide becomes too thick—leading to brittle failure or spallation—the wear performance should deteriorate. Supporting prior evidence includes observations from oxidation studies in HEAs and similar systems where moderate oxide formation improved performance in high-temperature environments. A falsifying result would be observing no correlation between the controlled Cu addition (and consequent oxide presence) and a measurable improvement in wear resistance or deformation, or if the expected oxide formation does not occur under the given operating regime.

families.principle: Directly manipulating the alloy composition (e.g., increasing Cu content) to control microstructural evolution and in‐situ oxidation during high‐temperature sliding, and correlating changes with measured wear and deformation.

predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation
specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis
cues_against: The hypothesis demands mechanistic insight, and a plain variable experiment may lack real-time mechanistic clarity.
families.best_lever: Implement a systematic Cu content variation in the FeNiCrCoCu HEA coating, then measure the evolution of the in‐situ formed oxide layer and its correlation with wear resistance and plastic deformation under ~600–800°C sliding conditions.

families.principle: Integrating controlled compositional experiments with complementary simulation work to correlate observed wear/deformation phenomena with atomistic mechanisms, thereby bridging the gap between empirical data and mechanistic understanding.
cues_for: controlled change relative to a baseline
cues_against: May be more complex and resource-intensive than single-technique approaches.
families.best_lever: Design an experimental campaign that variations Cu content in the HEA and evaluates wear and oxide layer integrity under high-temperature sliding, supported by simulations that detail the effect of Cu on dislocation interactions and oxide growth kinetics.

families.principle: Real‐time observation of the oxidation kinetics and deformation processes during high-temperature sliding using advanced microscopy or spectroscopy, to directly visualize oxide layer formation and dislocation interactions.
cues_against: The hypothesis requires a controlled change and directional prediction relative to a baseline, which pure characterization may not directly provide.
families.best_lever: Utilize high-temperature in situ TEM or environmental SEM to monitor the development of the oxide layer and related work hardening dynamics during sliding in real time.

families.principle: Computational modeling at the atomic or mesoscale to predict how a controlled compositional change affects dislocation dynamics, oxidation layer formation, and overall wear behavior under high temperatures.
cues_against: Prior attempts indicate the need for controlled experimental validation; simulations alone may not capture the full complexity of in-situ oxidation and subsequent mechanical effects.
families.best_lever: Conduct molecular dynamics or phase-field simulations that model dislocation behavior and oxide growth in response to incremental Cu additions, then compare predicted wear rates with experimental benchmarks.
